pos: n. (John Smyth, c. 1570–1612, English Separatist, founder of the first English Baptist congregation at Amsterdam)
etymology: English occupational surname Smith; John, from Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious.
biblical_def: John Smyth was a Cambridge fellow and lecturer at Lincoln who moved by stages out of the Church of England, through Separatism, into exile at Amsterdam about 1608. There he reached the conclusion that infant baptism is no baptism, dissolved his congregation, baptized himself and then the others, and so gathered what is reckoned the first English Baptist church. The self-baptism was irregular by any standard and he came to regret it, afterwards seeking membership among the Waterlander Mennonites and adopting with them a view of the will and of Christ's flesh the dictionary rejects. Thomas Helwys and a minority refused to follow him and returned to England. Smyth's permanent contribution is the argument, pressed from Scripture rather than from grievance, that baptism in the New Testament follows profession. Act 8:38 is his evidence in narrative: Philip and the eunuch “went down both into the water,” and the eunuch had confessed first. Mat 28:19 places the teaching and the baptizing in that order.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines baptism as the application of water to a person, as a sacrament or religious ceremony; and a separatist, as one that withdraws from a church.
webster_full: BAP'TISM, n. The application of water to a person, as a sacrament or religious ceremony, by which he is initiated into the visible church of Christ.
SEP'ARATIST, n. One that withdraws from a church, or rather from an established church, to which he has belonged; a dissenter.
IMMER'SION, n. The act of putting into a fluid below the surface; the state of sinking into a fluid.
scriptures: Act 8:38
And he commanded the chariot to stand still: and they went down both into the water, both Philip and the eunuch; and he baptized him.
Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost:
Rom 6:4
Therefore we are buried with him by baptism into death: that like as Christ was raised up from the dead by the glory of the Father, even so we also should walk in newness of life.
Act 2:42
And they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers.
corruption_summary: Smyth was right that baptism follows faith and wrong in nearly every step he took to act on it.
corruption_paragraphs: The self-baptism has rightly been criticized for centuries. A man cannot administer to himself an ordinance Christ gave to the church, and the irregularity bequeathed to Baptists an origin story they have had to explain ever since. Act 2:42 locates the ordinances inside the continuing fellowship of a gathered people, not in a private act of conscience. That Smyth saw the error and sought to repair it by joining the Mennonites only compounded it, since he then took on their errors about the person of Christ.

The argument itself, however, stands on its own feet and does not depend on its first advocate. Rom 6:4 explains baptism as burial with Christ into death and rising to newness of life, which assumes a person who has died with Him. Mat 28:19 joins discipling to baptizing. The Reformed Baptist position does not rest on Smyth; it rests on the texts, and the 1689 Confession states it without reference to him.

Greek sunthapto (G4916) — to bury together with; Romans 6:4.
Greek matheteuo (G3100) — to make a disciple; Matthew 28:19.
usage: “they went down both into the water” (Act 8:38) — the mode shown in narrative.
“Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them” (Mat 28:19) — the order of the commission.
“buried with him by baptism into death” (Rom 6:4) — what the ordinance signifies.

pos: n. (Thomas Helwys, c. 1575–c. 1616, English Baptist, founder of the first Baptist church on English soil and pioneer of religious liberty)
etymology: English Helwys, a Nottinghamshire surname; Thomas, from Aramaic Te'oma, a twin.
biblical_def: Thomas Helwys was a Nottinghamshire gentleman of Broxtowe Hall, trained at Gray's Inn, who funded and then shared the Amsterdam exile of John Smyth's congregation. When Smyth sought union with the Mennonites, Helwys refused, and about 1612 he led a dozen members back to England and gathered a church at Spitalfields outside London, the first Baptist congregation in the country. That year he published A Short Declaration of the Mistery of Iniquity, and sent a copy to King James with an inscription declaring that the king is a mortal man and has no authority over the immortal souls of his subjects. It is the first plea in English for liberty of conscience for all men, including, in his words, heretics, Turks and Jews. He was imprisoned in Newgate and died there within four years. Act 5:29 is the premise. Mat 22 renders to Caesar what is Caesar's, and the soul is not among those things. Rom 14 leaves each servant to stand or fall to his own master.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines conscience as internal or self-knowledge, and the faculty by which we judge of the moral rectitude of our own actions; and liberty, as freedom from restraint.
webster_full: CON'SCIENCE, n. Internal or self-knowledge, or judgment of right and wrong; or the faculty, power or principle within us, which decides on the lawfulness or unlawfulness of our own actions and affections.
LIB'ERTY, n. Freedom from restraint, in a general sense, and applicable to the body, or to the will or mind.
TOLERA'TION, n. The allowance of religious opinions and modes of worship in a state, when contrary to those of the established church.
scriptures: Act 5:29
Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men.
But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts: and be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear:
And fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul: but rather fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell.
Now then we are ambassadors for Christ, as though God did beseech you by us: we pray you in Christ's stead, be ye reconciled to God.
corruption_summary: Helwys told King James that a mortal man has no jurisdiction over immortal souls, and died in Newgate for the sentence.
corruption_paragraphs: Helwys drew his argument from the nature of faith rather than from a theory of rights. A magistrate can compel attendance, silence a preacher, and fine a recusant; he cannot create belief, because belief is the soul's response to God and the soul is outside his commission. Mat 10:28 draws the same boundary from the other side, distinguishing what man can kill from what he cannot touch. 1Pe 3:15 commissions the believer to give an answer with meekness and fear, which assumes persuasion as the church's only proper instrument.

The modern misuse of Helwys is to enlist him for the claim that all religions are equally true or that the state must treat truth and error as indistinguishable. He believed nothing of the kind; he thought Rome and Islam damning errors and said so in the same book. His argument was that error is answered by preaching and not by prison. 2Co 5:20 gives the church its office, ambassadors who beseech, and an ambassador who reaches for the magistrate's sword has abandoned the embassy.
roots_summary: Greek suneidesis (G4893), conscience; presbeuo (G4243), to act as ambassador; apologia (G627), an answer, a defence.
roots_lines: Greek peitharcheo (G3980) — to obey one in authority; Acts 5:29.
Greek apologia (G627) — a verbal defence, an answer; 1 Peter 3:15.
Greek presbeuo (G4243) — to be an ambassador; 2 Corinthians 5:20.
usage: “We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29) — written to a king, from Newgate.
“be ready always to give an answer” (1Pe 3:15) — persuasion, not compulsion.
“we are ambassadors for Christ” (2Co 5:20) — the church's only office toward unbelievers.

pos: n. (Henry Barrow, c. 1550–1593, English Separatist, hanged at Tyburn for writings against the established church)
etymology: English Barrow, from Old English beorg, a hill or burial mound; Henry, Germanic, ruler of the home.
biblical_def: Henry Barrow was a Cambridge man and Gray's Inn lawyer of worldly habits who was converted, by his own account, on walking into a London church out of curiosity. He joined the Separatist cause, was arrested in 1586 while visiting John Greenwood in the Clink, and spent nearly seven years in prison, writing. With Greenwood he set out the fullest early case for the gathered church: that a true church consists of believers voluntarily joined by covenant, governed by its own officers under Christ alone, with no parish boundaries, no bishops and no royal supremacy in spiritual things. The writings were smuggled to Dort and printed. In April 1593 he and Greenwood were hanged at Tyburn for devising and circulating seditious books. Mat 18:20 is the ground he stood on, that where two or three are gathered together in Christ's name, there He is in the midst. 1Pe 2:9 is the dignity he claimed for ordinary believers, a chosen generation and a royal priesthood.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a church as a congregation of Christians associated in one body; and sedition, as a factious commotion of the people.
webster_full: CHURCH, n. A congregation of Christians associated in one body, in a particular place, united under one form of ecclesiastical government.
SEDI'TION, n. A factious commotion of the people, a tumultuous assembly of men rising in opposition to law or the administration of justice.
INDEPEND'ENT, n. One who in religious affairs maintains that every congregation of Christians is a complete church.
scriptures: For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them.
But ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people; that ye should shew forth the praises of him who hath called you out of darkness into his marvellous light:
Act 2:42
And they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers.
And I say also unto thee, That thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.
corruption_summary: Barrow argued that a church is a gathered company under Christ, and the state hanged him for the sentence.
corruption_paragraphs: The Elizabethan charge against Barrow was sedition, not heresy, and the charge was in its way accurate. To deny that the parish is the church and that the sovereign is its governor was to deny the constitutional settlement of the realm. Mat 16:18 is where the collision begins, for Christ says “I will build my church,” in the first person and the future tense, and a church He builds is not a department of state.

The modern distortion of Barrow is to treat the gathered-church principle as a licence for churchless Christianity, as though believers may assemble informally and dispense with officers, membership and discipline. Barrow taught the opposite: he wanted the covenant explicit, the officers elected, the discipline exercised. Act 2:42 lists what the gathered company continued in, and all four items require a visible, ordered congregation.
roots_summary: Greek ekklesia (G1577), an assembly called out; sunago (G4863), to gather together; basileios (G934), royal.
roots_lines: Greek ekklesia (G1577) — a called-out assembly, a church; Matthew 16:18.
Greek genos (G1085) — a race, a generation, a kind; 1 Peter 2:9.
usage: “where two or three are gathered together in my name” (Mat 18:20) — the gathered church.
“a chosen generation, a royal priesthood” (1Pe 2:9) — said of ordinary members.
“upon this rock I will build my church” (Mat 16:18) — whose church it is.

pos: n. (Scrooby, a village in north Nottinghamshire; the manor house where the Pilgrim congregation was gathered about 1606)
etymology: Old Norse personal name with Old English by, a farmstead or settlement.
biblical_def: Scrooby was a village on the Great North Road with an old archbishop's manor house, whose bailiff was William Brewster. About 1606 a Separatist congregation began meeting in that house, drawing people from Scrooby, Babworth, Austerfield and Gainsborough; Richard Clyfton preached, John Robinson assisted, and a teenage William Bradford walked over from Austerfield each Lord's Day. Under pressure from the ecclesiastical courts the congregation determined to leave the realm, was betrayed on a first attempt at Boston in 1607, and reached Amsterdam in 1608 before settling at Leiden. From Leiden a portion of them sailed in 1620 and founded Plymouth. The whole New England enterprise is traceable to a farmhouse congregation of perhaps a few dozen people. Mat 18:20 is the warrant such a company had for existing. Heb 10:25 is the obligation that made them meet in a manor house when the parish church was closed to them.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a conventicle as an assembly of dissenters from the established church, for religious worship; and a pilgrim, as a wanderer; a traveler.
webster_full: CONVEN'TICLE, n. An assembly of dissenters from the established church, for religious worship.
PIL'GRIM, n. A wanderer; a traveler; particularly, one that travels to a distance from his own country to visit a holy place.
MAN'OR, n. The land belonging to a lord or nobleman, or so much land as a lord or great personage kept in his own hands.
scriptures: For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them.
Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is; but exhorting one another: and so much the more, as ye see the day approaching.
(Of whom the world was not worthy:) they wandered in deserts, and in mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth.
Act 2:42
And they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers.
corruption_summary: A few dozen Nottinghamshire villagers in a bailiff's house became, in fourteen years, the Plymouth colony.
corruption_paragraphs: Scrooby is the standing argument against despising small congregations. Nothing about the gathering in that manor house was impressive by any measure a modern church would apply. Mat 18:20 attaches the promise of Christ's presence to two or three, which is a deliberate number; it names the smallest plausible assembly and gives it everything. The church-growth instinct that measures a congregation by its weight is measuring the wrong thing.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Heb 10:25's obligation under cost. The Scrooby people met when meeting was illegal, lost property and liberty for it, and then crossed an ocean rather than stop. A church that treats attendance as optional when the only cost is inconvenience has not understood what the verse was written to address.
roots_summary: Greek sunago (G4863), to gather; episunagoge (G1997), assembling together; parepidemos, a sojourner.
roots_lines: Greek episunagoge (G1997) — a gathering together, assembling; Hebrews 10:25.
Greek egkataleipo (G1459) — to forsake, to abandon; Hebrews 10:25.
usage: “where two or three are gathered together in my name” (Mat 18:20) — a manor-house congregation.
“Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together” (Heb 10:25) — obeyed at real cost.
“they wandered in deserts” (Heb 11:38) — and then across an ocean.

pos: n. (John Robinson, c. 1576–1625, pastor of the Separatist congregation at Leiden, spiritual father of the Pilgrims)
etymology: English patronymic, son of Robin; John, from Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious.
biblical_def: John Robinson was a Cambridge fellow deprived for nonconformity who joined the Scrooby congregation, went with it to Amsterdam and then to Leiden, and pastored it there from 1609 until his death. He was the ablest Separatist theologian of his generation and the most moderate: he debated the Arminians at Leiden on the Reformed side, defended infant baptism against the Baptists, and over the years softened his refusal of communion with godly members of the Church of England. When the Mayflower company left in 1620 he remained with the larger part of the congregation, intending to follow, and died before he could. His farewell charge, as Edward Winslow recorded it, urged the emigrants to expect further light to break forth out of God's holy word — a sentence often quoted as if it licensed novelty, though Robinson meant further light out of the word and not beyond it. Act 17:11 is the Berean practice he commended. Isa 8:20 is the limit he assumed.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a pastor as a minister of the gospel who has the charge of a church and congregation; and to expound, as to explain; to lay open the meaning.
webster_full: PAS'TOR, n. A minister of the gospel who has the charge of a church and congregation, whose duty is to watch over the people of his charge.
EXPOUND', v.t. To explain; to lay open the meaning; to clear of obscurity; to interpret.
FAREWELL', n. A wish of happiness or welfare at parting; the parting compliment.
scriptures: These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.
Isa 8:20
To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood.
John 17:17
Sanctify them through thy truth: thy word is truth.
corruption_summary: Robinson's farewell charge is quoted for its openness and was spoken by a man with a very firm floor under his feet.
corruption_paragraphs: The sentence about further light is one of the most misused in church history. It is cited to justify revising doctrines the church has always held, as though revelation continued. Robinson said light would break forth out of God's holy word, and he had spent his career demonstrating what he meant: patient exposition yielding understanding the previous generation had missed, within the text. Isa 8:20 is the test he would have applied to any claimed new light, that if they speak not according to this word there is no light in them.

The second misuse is to make Robinson a patron of doctrinal minimalism because he grew more charitable toward the English parishes. His charity was toward persons, not propositions; he went on contending against Arminianism and against believers' baptism to the end. Act 20:28 gives the pastor's charge, to take heed to himself and to all the flock, and a shepherd who will not say which pastures are poisoned has not taken heed.
roots_summary: Greek poimen (G4166), shepherd; anakrino (G350), to examine; hagiazo (G37), to sanctify.
roots_lines: Greek anakrino (G350) — to examine, to sift, to search; Acts 17:11.
Greek poimaino (G4165) — to feed, to shepherd; Acts 20:28.
Greek hagiazo (G37) — to sanctify, to set apart; John 17:17.
usage: “searched the scriptures daily” (Act 17:11) — where further light comes from.
“if they speak not according to this word” (Isa 8:20) — the test of any new light.
“Sanctify them through thy truth: thy word is truth” (John 17:17) — the floor under the farewell.

pos: n. pl. (the English Separatist congregation resident at Leiden in Holland, 1609–1620, under John Robinson)
etymology: Leiden, a Dutch city on the Old Rhine; separatist, from Latin separare, to set apart.
biblical_def: The Leiden Separatists were the Scrooby congregation after it left Amsterdam, where the quarrels of the older English exile church had alarmed them. At Leiden they found a university town that tolerated them, trades that would employ them, and eleven years of relative peace under John Robinson's ministry. The peace was not comfortable: they worked at wool-combing and printing for poor wages, their children were drawn into Dutch life and into the garrison, and a renewed war with Spain threatened. In 1620 a minority sailed for Virginia in the Speedwell and Mayflower; most stayed, and the Leiden church continued some years after Robinson's death. Their decision to leave was not persecution but the fear of being absorbed, which is a quieter danger and has undone more congregations. Heb 11:38 covers the whole episode. 1Pe 2:9 names what they believed themselves to be, a people called out of darkness into His marvellous light.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to separate as to disunite; to divide; to sever; and an exile, as the state of being expelled from one's native country.
webster_full: SEP'ARATE, v.t. To disunite; to divide; to sever; to part, in almost any manner.
EX'ILE, n. Banishment; the state of being expelled from one's native country or place of residence by authority.
SO'JOURN, v.i. To dwell for a time; to dwell or live in a place as a temporary resident.
scriptures: (Of whom the world was not worthy:) they wandered in deserts, and in mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth.
But ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people; that ye should shew forth the praises of him who hath called you out of darkness into his marvellous light:
Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is; but exhorting one another: and so much the more, as ye see the day approaching.
For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them.
corruption_summary: Leiden gave them toleration and nearly dissolved them, which persecution had failed to do.
corruption_paragraphs: The Leiden years are the most instructive part of the Pilgrim story because nothing dramatic happened in them. No one was imprisoned; the congregation simply watched its young people drift into Dutch trades, Dutch marriages and Dutch indifference, and concluded that it would not survive another generation on those terms. 1Pe 2:9 calls the church a peculiar people, and peculiarity is precisely what toleration erodes.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that assimilation is a form of defeat, and a congregation at ease should examine itself more carefully than one under pressure. Heb 10:25 was not the Leiden problem; they kept assembling. The problem was that assembling had become one activity among many in lives otherwise indistinguishable from their neighbours', and they had the honesty to see it.
roots_summary: Greek peripoiesis (G4047), a peculiar possession; skotos (G4655), darkness; planao (G4105), to wander.
roots_lines: Greek peripoiesis (G4047) — a purchased possession, a peculiar people; 1 Peter 2:9.
usage: “Of whom the world was not worthy” (Heb 11:38) — eleven years of wool-combing.
“a peculiar people” (1Pe 2:9) — what toleration was dissolving.
“out of darkness into his marvellous light” (1Pe 2:9) — their own account of themselves.

pos: n. (the colony planted at Plymouth in New England, 1620, by the Leiden Separatists and their fellow passengers)
etymology: Plymouth, the English port of departure; plantation, from Latin plantare, to plant.
biblical_def: Plymouth Plantation was founded in December 1620 by about a hundred passengers, fewer than half of them from the Leiden church, who had been blown north of their Virginia patent and settled on Cape Cod Bay. Because they were outside the bounds of their charter the adult males signed a compact in the ship's cabin, covenanting themselves into a civil body politic for the general good — the congregational church covenant applied to the ordering of a commonwealth. Half the company died the first winter. The colony survived on Indian corn, a treaty with Massasoit, and uncommon stubbornness, was never large or rich, and was absorbed into Massachusetts Bay in 1691. Its importance is out of all proportion to its size, because the pattern of a covenanted self-governing community was carried from it into American political life. Psa 127:1 is the sentence Bradford's history keeps proving: “Except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it.”
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a plantation as the place planted; applied to a colony; and a compact, as an agreement; a contract between parties.
webster_full: PLANTA'TION, n. The place planted; applied to a colony or to a cultivated estate.
COM'PACT, n. An agreement; a contract between parties; a word that may be applied, in a general sense, to any covenant or contract between individuals.
COL'ONY, n. A company of people transplanted from their mother country to a remote province or country.
scriptures: A Song of degrees for Solomon. Except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it: except the LORD keep the city, the watchman waketh but in vain.
(Of whom the world was not worthy:) they wandered in deserts, and in mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth.
He that goeth forth and weepeth, bearing precious seed, shall doubtless come again with rejoicing, bringing his sheaves with him.
Therefore, my beloved brethren, be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord.
corruption_summary: A hundred people, half dead by spring, planted the political habit of covenanting a community under God.
corruption_paragraphs: Two opposite distortions of Plymouth are current. The first makes the Pilgrims the founders of a Christian nation by deliberate design, which overstates what a struggling fishing settlement intended. The second makes them merely economic migrants with religious decoration, which ignores their own documents. Psa 127:1 is quoted here because Bradford's own account reads that way: he attributes the survival to providence and the failures to sin, and keeps doing so for thirty years.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is in 1Co 15:58, that labour in the Lord is not in vain even when its visible fruit is small. Plymouth was eclipsed within a decade by Massachusetts Bay and swallowed in seventy years. Psa 126:6 promises that he who goes out weeping, bearing precious seed, shall come again with rejoicing, and the harvest in view is not always the sower's own.
roots_summary: Hebrew banah (H1129), to build; zera (H2233), seed; Greek kopos (G2873), labour.
roots_lines: Hebrew shaw (H7723) — vanity, emptiness, in vain; Psalm 127:1.
usage: “Except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it” (Psa 127:1) — Bradford's refrain.
“bearing precious seed” (Psa 126:6) — a harvest later than the sower.
“your labour is not in vain in the Lord” (1Co 15:58) — said over a colony that vanished.

pos: n. (William Bradford, 1590–1657, governor of Plymouth Colony for most of thirty-six years, author of Of Plymouth Plantation)
etymology: Old English brad ford, the broad ford; William, Germanic, resolute protector.
biblical_def: William Bradford was an orphaned Yorkshire farm boy who walked to the Scrooby meetings as a teenager, went into exile at Amsterdam and Leiden, sailed on the Mayflower, lost his wife overboard in Cape Cod harbour, and was elected governor of Plymouth in the spring of 1621 after the first governor died. He was re-elected thirty times. His history, Of Plymouth Plantation, written over decades and unpublished until the nineteenth century, is the finest piece of prose any English colonist produced and the most candid: it records the colony's quarrels, its debts, its failures of charity and the author's own griefs with the same unhurried plainness as its deliverances. He taught himself Hebrew late in life, wanting to see “with mine own eyes” the language God spoke. Heb 11:38 is the chapter he consciously wrote under. 1Co 15:58 is the conviction that kept him at the work.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a governor as one who governs; one invested with supreme authority to administer the laws; and a history, as a narration of facts and events.
webster_full: GOV'ERNOR, n. One who governs, rules or directs; one invested with supreme authority to administer or enforce the laws.
HIS'TORY, n. An account of facts, particularly of facts respecting nations or states; a narration of events in the order in which they happened.
PIL'GRIM, n. A wanderer; a traveler; one that travels to a distance from his own country.
scriptures: (Of whom the world was not worthy:) they wandered in deserts, and in mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth.
Therefore, my beloved brethren, be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord.
A Song of degrees for Solomon. Except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it: except the LORD keep the city, the watchman waketh but in vain.
Heb 13:8
Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever.
corruption_summary: Thirty-six years of governing a poor colony, and the prose of the man who did it is still the best account of any of them.
corruption_paragraphs: Bradford's candour is a model that Christian institutional history rarely follows. He records the colony's decision to abandon common stock after it bred idleness, the scandal of the Wessagusset settlement, the debt that crushed the plantation for twenty years, and the drift of families away from the town he loved. He does not tidy any of it. Act 20 required a minister to declare the whole counsel of God; a Christian historian owes the whole account of the facts.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. What it faces is partisan use: Bradford is conscripted by one side as the founder of a godly republic and by another as a colonial oppressor, and neither reads him. The principle to recover is Heb 13:8, which Bradford leaned on as his settlement changed past recognition — Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever — the one fixed point in a history of loss.
roots_summary: Greek planao (G4105), to wander; kopos (G2873), labour; semeron (G4594), to day.
usage: “Of whom the world was not worthy” (Heb 11:38) — the chapter he wrote under.
“be ye stedfast, unmoveable” (1Co 15:58) — thirty-six elections.
“Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever” (Heb 13:8) — the fixed point.

pos: n. (the Somerset Confession of 1656, a Particular Baptist confession issued by sixteen churches in the west of England)
etymology: Somerset, Old English, the settlers about the summer dwelling; confession, from Latin confiteri, to acknowledge.
biblical_def: The Somerset Confession was drawn up in 1656 by sixteen Particular Baptist congregations in Somerset, Devon, Dorset and Wiltshire, and runs to forty-six articles. It is less celebrated than the First and Second London Confessions and more revealing of the ordinary western churches, who were closer to the Independents and the Army than the London men were, and who wrote in a plainer idiom. It confesses the Trinity, particular redemption, justification by faith, believers' baptism by immersion, congregational government with elders and deacons, the laying on of hands after baptism, and the lawfulness of the magistrate. Its purpose was to show that these churches held the catholic faith and were not the anarchists their neighbours took them for. Jude 1:3 is the duty discharged. 2Ti 1:13 is the method. 1Ti 3:15 supplies the reason a local association puts its faith in writing at all: the church is the pillar and ground of the truth, and a pillar must be visible.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a confession of faith as a public avowal of belief; and association, as a society formed for transacting business or promoting some object.
webster_full: CONFES'SION, n. Profession; avowal of a religious faith. A formulary in which the articles of faith are comprised.
ASSOCIA'TION, n. Union of persons in a company or society for some particular purpose; a society formed for transacting business.
AR'TICLE, n. A point of faith; a distinct proposition in a connected series of such propositions.
scriptures: Jude 1:3

Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints.
Hold fast the form of sound words, which thou hast heard of me, in faith and love which is in Christ Jesus.
But if I tarry long, that thou mayest know how thou oughtest to behave thyself in the house of God, which is the church of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth.
Act 2:42
And they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers.
corruption_summary: Sixteen west-country churches put their faith in writing to prove they were Christians and not insurrectionists.
corruption_paragraphs: The Somerset churches wrote under a particular suspicion: that Baptists were Münster reborn, levellers in religion who would overturn the magistrate and the family together. The confession answers by stating the catholic doctrines first and the distinctive ones afterwards, which is the right order and is still the right order. A church known chiefly for what it denies has let its opponents choose its subject.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live temptation is the opposite of 1656: congregations that decline to publish any confession at all, on the ground that doctrinal statements repel visitors. 1Ti 3:15 makes the church the pillar and ground of the truth, and Act 2:42 lists doctrine first among the things the first church continued in. The principle to recover is that an association of churches owes the public a plain account of what it believes.

“the pillar and ground of the truth” (1Ti 3:15) — why a church publishes.
“continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine” (Act 2:42) — doctrine named first.

pos: n. (the Orthodox Creed of 1679, a General Baptist confession drawn up in Buckinghamshire to unite Protestants against Rome)
etymology: Greek orthodoxos, right in opinion; creed, from Latin credo, I believe.
biblical_def: The Orthodox Creed was adopted in 1679 by General Baptist churches in Buckinghamshire, Oxfordshire, Hertfordshire and Bedfordshire, and is the most catholic-minded confession the English Baptists produced. Its fifty articles embrace the Apostles', Nicene and Athanasian Creeds by name and print them in full, affirm the Trinity in the strictest terms, and were framed expressly to unite all true Protestants against what its authors called the error and idolatry of Rome. Its soteriology is Arminian, and the dictionary dissents from it there; but its Trinitarian rigour was aimed at a real danger among General Baptists, some of whom were already sliding toward the Socinianism that would hollow out much of that connexion in the next century. The instinct was sound even where the soteriology was not. Jude 1:3 is the article's warrant. 1Ti 3:15 is the church's office in holding it. John 14:6 and Act 4:12 mark the exclusivity the General Baptists at least retained.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a creed as a brief authoritative form of religious belief; and orthodox, as sound in the Christian faith; believing the genuine doctrines taught in the Scriptures.
webster_full: CREED, n. A brief authoritative form of religious belief; a summary of the articles of Christian faith.
OR'THODOX, a. Sound in the Christian faith; believing the genuine doctrines taught in the Scriptures.
SOCIN'IANISM, n. The tenets or doctrines of Socinus, who denied the divinity of Christ.
scriptures: Jude 1:3

Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints.
But if I tarry long, that thou mayest know how thou oughtest to behave thyself in the house of God, which is the church of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth.
John 14:6
Jesus saith unto him, I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me.
Act 4:12
Neither is there salvation in any other: for there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved.
corruption_summary: A General Baptist confession that prints the Athanasian Creed in full was defending against a real and coming collapse.
corruption_paragraphs: History vindicated the alarm. Within two generations much of the General Baptist connexion had gone Unitarian, and the churches that survived orthodox were those that had taken the Trinity as a boundary and not as an inheritance. The Orthodox Creed's decision to reprint the ancient symbols was a judgement that the doctrine could not be assumed. 1Ti 3:15 charges the church with upholding the truth, and a truth upheld only by habit is upheld by nothing.

The dictionary names the confession's Arminianism as error, not as a variant. A conditional election grounded in foreseen faith reverses Scripture's own order and makes grace answerable to the creature's will. That said, the Orthodox Creed illustrates an important fact: the fence around the Trinity and the fence around the gospel are different fences, and a church may hold the first while its hold on the second is defective. Act 4:12 is a boundary both parties confessed.
